title: Rereading chapters 1–4
hookLine: reread the twin verses, earnestness, thought, flowers
tomorrow: the old verses have a fool and a wise one. which one is you?

lines: A SONG IN THE GROCERY STORE.
cards: A song from years ago comes on in the grocery store, and a line you sang over and over suddenly means something, because now you've lived it. The words didn't change. You did.

That's today: back to the Dhammapada, the old book of the Buddha's verses, chapters one to four: the twin verses, earnestness, thought and flowers. Same pages, after two weeks on the far shore. Different reader.
So what jumps out this time that didn't before?

teach.h: ALL THAT WE ARE: OUR THOUGHTS.
teach.b: Open to the first verse, in Max Müller's translation: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts."
After weeks of poems about views, that line lands differently. The teachers in the square, each calling theirs true, were made up of their thoughts too.
Turn to chapter two, earnestness: "Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvana), thoughtlessness the path of death."

teach.h: AN ISLAND NO FLOOD CAN OVERWHELM.
teach.b: And a few verses on, something that wasn't there before, or was and waited: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm."
An island, and a flood. Kappa asked for exactly that, and now the old verse answers back. Chapter three compares the wavering mind to an arrow a fletcher straightens.
Chapter four, flowers, says fine words that aren't lived are like a bright flower with no scent.
That's rereading: new verses in old pages. And look how this fortnight gathers: cross yourself, what I rely on, the island, stilled, look on it as empty, I follow in mind.
Each one makes an old line a little louder, the way a friend's voice is easier to pick out once you know it. The pages wait. The reader comes back changed.

how: Buddhists return to the Dhammapada again and again; some recite a few verses daily or learn them by heart, and teachers often pick a verse to open a talk.

o: a second look at the Dhammapada's opening chapters
a quiz on the Dhammapada's verses in their order
a lesson on copying the Dhammapada in Pali script

games.q: the Dhammapada, chapters 1–4 — tap the pairs.
p: all that we are: what we have thought

s: rereading a text you know is a waste; you've already got what's in it
the pages stay the same, but the reader changes: Kappa's island makes verse 25 land in a new way.
a verse in the Dhammapada's chapter on earnestness speaks of an island no flood can overwhelm
by rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island.

games.q: you rewatch a movie from middle school with your little cousin and catch a line you'd never noticed. your cousin says 'it was always there.' what does today's reading say?
o: it was there, but you weren't the reader yet who could hear it.
you missed it before because you weren't paying attention at all.
the movie got better; somebody must have changed it.
games.why: new verses in old pages: the words don't change, the reader does. a line waits until the life arrives that can hear it.

practice: If there's paper nearby, copy one line from today by hand, the one that caught you, slowly, in your own writing. Then read it back once, as if someone else had written it for you.
Ask what it says to the person you are this week, and sit with that, breathing easily, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Rereading chapters 1 to 4 of the Dhammapada: the twin verses, earnestness, thought and flowers, opened again by a reader who has crossed a few floods since the first time through.

orig.note: Pali: earnestness, heedfulness; the title word of the Dhammapada's second chapter.

carryVoice: To keep on the shelf: new verses in old pages, waiting for the next reader you become. Two weeks, gathered.
